rich_text.plain_text: The bedroom is the only room you look at while lying down, and almost nobody styles it that way. The art goes above the headboard, where the only people who ever see it are guests passing the open door.

rich_text.plain_text: That is not a reason to leave the headboard wall bare. It is a reason to think about two walls instead of one.

rich_text.plain_text: The wall above the bed is the one that frames the room from the doorway. It wants presence: one substantial piece, or a considered pair, centred on the bed.

text.content: The wall above the bed is the one that frames the room from the doorway. It wants presence: one substantial piece, or a considered pair, centred on the bed.

rich_text.plain_text: The wall opposite the bed is the one you actually look at, twice a day, at your least critical and most receptive. It can afford to be gentler and more personal. A single quiet print here does more for how the room feels than anything above your head ever will.

rich_text.plain_text: Leave roughly 20 to 25 cm between the top of the headboard and the bottom of the frame. Any higher and the art floats off on its own; any lower and it looks like it slipped.

rich_text.plain_text: Aim for the art to span about two thirds of the bed's width. Above a double, a single portrait print can look stranded. A pair, or one large piece, holds the wall.

rich_text.plain_text: Centre the arrangement on the bed, not on the wall. Beds are rarely dead centre once you have allowed for a door or a radiator, and the eye reads the bed as the middle of the room regardless.

rich_text.plain_text: When there is no wall to spare, stop hanging and start leaning. A print propped on a chest of drawers or a low shelf, overlapping a lamp or a stack of books, gives the room art without another set of holes in the plaster. It also lets you swap it in ten seconds, which is the real luxury.
